Vs.

full_judgment:
2. Plaintiffs respondents filed the suit being T. S. No. 270 of 1973 in the Court of Munsif, Goalundo, Faridpur for declaration of title and confirmation of possession against appellants and respondents No. 3 to 5. The suit land originally belonged to Gaya Nath and Kanai Lal. Gaya Nath died leaving behind a widow Kiranbala and a son the plaintiff and a daughter defendant No. 1. Kanailal used to look after the interest of the minor plaintiff, defendant No.1 and their mother after the death of Gaya Nath. The plaintiff alleged that Kanailal intentionally defaulted in payment of rent and the holding was about to be sold in auction. In order to save the property Kiran Bala as guardian of the plaintiff executed a patta dated 13-11-1940 in favour of defendant No.1 in respect of 'Ka' schedule land as a benami transaction. The S.A. and R.S. records stand in the name of defendant No.1 but the plaintiff contended that they had been all along in possession. Plaintiff brought the suit since the defendants are threatening to dispossess the plaintiff particularly defendants Nos. 2 to 5 who have been giving out that they have purchased the property from defendant No.1 Hence the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession. 

 3. The suit was contested by defendants, 2 to 5 by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit is barred by limitation, that the suit land has been sold by defendant No. 1 to defendants 2 to 5 by two kabalas dated 11-4-73 and since purchase the defendants are in possession of the suit land. It is contended that the patta dated 13-11-40 was a genuine transaction and not a benami transaction, as alleged by the plaintiff. 

 4. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal by the defendants the learned Subordinate Judge set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and allowed the appeal. The appellate Court below found on evidence that possession was with the defendants and the record of right it has correctly reflected that the defendant was in possession. In this view of the matter the appellate Court below dismissed the suit. In second appeal the High Court Division considered that the Patta Ext. 1 came from the custody of the plaintiff and no satisfactory explanation was given as to how it came from them. The High Court Division took the view that the purchase of the defendants 2 to 5 was not bonafide nor for valuable consideration. So far as possession is concerned the High Court Division found the possession of the plaintiff and not with the defendants as found by the appellate Court below. No decision, however, was given on the point of limitation. 

 6. Defendants 2 to 5 are the appellants. As it has been noted that they relied on two kabalas dated 11-4-73 and their contention was that since the date of purchase the defendants are in possession of the suit land and they are bonafide purchaser of the suit land for value and the Patta dated 13-11-40 was not a benami transaction. It was a genuine transaction in favour of defendant No. 1 who had sold the land to the defendants 2 to 5 and validly conferred title on them. The High Court Division gave a stress to the fact that the Patta Ext. 1 was produced by the plaintiff and no explanation was given as to how it was in the custody of the plaintiff and therefore the contention that it was benami transaction is well grounded. This view is not supported by evidence because D.W.I stated that during rent-roll operation he gave the Patta to the plaintiff and P.W. 2. This evidence clearly show that the Patla surfaced only 10/11 years ago. The evidence is that the plaintiff was a minor boy in 1940. The appellate Court below took notice of the fact that such a young boy could not have obtained a registered Patta from Sub-Registrar's Office. Then the evidence of P.W. 1 Kiran Bala was considered who stated that her husband Gaya Nath died in 1935 when the plaintiff was only about 2 years old. This puts the age of the boy, the plaintiff, between 6/7 years in 1940. The plaintiff P.W. 2 himself stated in cross-examination that he saw Patta only 10/11 years ago for the first time. The evidence of P.W. 1 Bhabendra Nath was that during the rent roll operation he gave the Patta Ext. 1 to the plaintiff. P.W. 4 admitted in cross-examination that he was not present when the Patta in dispute was granted. The oral evidence lead to irresistible conclusion that the Patta was not a benami one as contended by the plaintiff. This view of the appellate court is well founded and therefore the view that prevailed with the High Court Division as to how the Patta came from the plaintiffs side was satisfactorily explained by defendant. Moreover, the onus of benami is on the plaintiff inasmuch as it is the plaintiff who took this plea. It is well settled that Benami transaction will be scrutinised by the Court very carefully and unless it is established firmly no transaction should by termed as benami. The contention that the Patta was granted in benami in 1940 but the plaintiff have not adduced any evidence as what happened between 1940 and 1965. In record of right the name of the defendant No. 1 has been shown. The contention of the plaintiff that the patta was granted to save the property from the auction sale is belied by Ext.3 which is a statement in Rent Execution Case No. 633 of 1942. It shows that the execution case being Execution Case No.633 of 1943 arose out of decree dated 18-11-41 passed in Rent Suit No. 973 of 1941. This glaring fact was noticed by the appellate Court below and it has considered that if the Rent Suit was filed in 1941 and the decree was passed towards the latter part of that year, how a Patta could be granted in 1940 purportedly for saving the property which was not in danger at that time. The appellate Court below rightly noticed that it could not be contemplation of the plaintiff (who was a boy of 7/8 years old) or his mother in 1940 that there will be a Rent Suit In 1941 in Execution of which the suit land might be put to auction sale. This fact stares in the face of the plaintiff's case and therefore the imaginary plea of benami nature of the Patta does not bear scrutiny. 

 7. Having cleared this point on the question of benami transaction the next question that demands consideration as to possession. The evidence of P.W. 1 and P.W. 3 in cross-examination clearly establishes the possession of the defendants at least for the last 4 years. So when the suit was brought obviously the plaintiff was not in possession and therefore the prayer for confirmation of possession has no leg to stand. Evidence of the Bargadars D.W. 2 and 3 clearly demolishes the case of the plaintiff and the corroborative evidence is that of P.W.S 4 and 5 who were relied on by the appellate Court below as neutral witness. D.W. 2 is a man of 70 years old. He deposed that he was present, at the time of talk of the purchase of the suit land by defendants 2 to 5. P.W. 3 Muslim stated that his father cultivated the land as borgadar under defendant No.2. D.W. 3 himself borga cultivated the Suitland for 10/12 years before their purchase. D.Ws. 4 and 5 have lands contiguous to the suit land and they were naturally competent enough to speak about possession of the suit land. The cumulative effect of such evidence is that the possession of the defendants was well established. "Where there are benami transactions and the question is who is the real owner, the actual possession or receipt of the rents of the property is most important" (Imambandi Begum V. Kumbewani Prasad 13 I.A. 160.) In this case the plaintiffs produced the dakhilas which showed that rents were paid through them as 'Marfatdars'. Payment of rent by the plaintiff as 'Marfatdars' could not constitute recognition of them, as tenants. Naba Chandra V. Nanda Kumar, 2 D.L.R. 552(556). Be it noted that defendant No.1 is the sister of the plaintiff and that makes the case of the defendant more probable that the transaction was genuine and the patta was not benami as claimed by the plaintiff. The onus was on the plaintiff to produce whether what was prima facie, the nature of the transaction was really not so. The plaintiff did not make any such prayer in the suit either that the Patta was a benami transaction. The High Court Division unfortunately overlooked this fact established on evidence. The defendant No. 1 has sold to defendants 2 to 5 by three kabalas dated 11-4-73. If the benami transaction is disbelieved ,as it has been, then the defendant No.1 could validly confer title on defendants 2 to 5 Thus the title of the defendants is established and the fact of possession as well. Therefore the plaintiff's suit is devoid of any substance and must be dismissed. The reasonings of the High Court Division do not stand inasmuch as in a suit for title and confirmation of possession brought by the plaintiff, none of it could be found in his favour. The decision of the High Court Division therefore must be set aside.
